header.property: properties/123456789 (web stream for the site; 3 test streams ignored)

executive_summary.biggest_strength: A clear three-plan ladder: the middle plan is badged, and each step up costs less per unit of capacity.
executive_summary.biggest_blocker: Nothing on the page records a plan choice, so no change can be measured.
executive_summary.quick_win: Add a plan-click event on the buttons and a short FAQ under the cards.
executive_summary.at_stake: 57 visitors viewed pricing in 30 days (directional: under 100 pricing views); 0 plan choices were recorded, and 63% of the next pages they opened were the integrations list.

scorecard.key_number: 12 key events defined (4 of them test events), 0 fired; 26 low days, tracking complete only from 2026-10-01 (4 of 30 days, under 7, so the full window is kept and Part A is directional)
scorecard.why: Conversions can't be read from this property yet, and most of the window predates complete tracking.

scorecard.key_number: 15% of sessions include a pricing view (62 of 400) (directional: under 100 pricing views)
scorecard.why: Pricing is well found; the home page is the main way in.

scorecard.key_number: 12s engagement per view vs 10s site; read-to-bottom 16% vs 22% site (directional: under 100 pricing views)
scorecard.why: Visitors spend longer here than on an average page, but fewer reach the bottom, where the comparison table and sales link sit.

scorecard.key_number: 63% of next-page views go to one features or integrations page, the integrations list (directional: under 100 pricing views)
scorecard.why: Most visitors who leave pricing for another page go to check the integrations list: the page doesn't answer "does it work with my tools?".

scorecard.key_number: 0 plan-button clicks recorded; outbound clicks on, but every sign-up link points to an app subdomain (directional: under 100 pricing views)
scorecard.why: No plan choice is visible in GA4, so no change to this page can be measured.

scorecard.key_number: 5 mobile pricing views, under the 30 needed
scorecard.why: Too few mobile views to judge.

scorecard.key_number: 3 plans named by audience or stage; each step costs about 3x the price for about 4x the capacity; spread top ÷ entry about 10x
scorecard.why: A clean three-step ladder with clear audience names: each plan costs less per unit of capacity than the one below.

scorecard.key_number: top plan shown beside the others; annual saving labelled in months, not money, worth over 25% off (generous: check the margin); monthly selected by default; no crossed-out price, no alternative-cost comparison, no value or ROI figure (noted, not graded)
scorecard.why: A visible top plan and a generous annual saving.

scorecard.key_number: all 3 cards list the same short list, all features rather than outcomes; nothing on the cards is gated to a higher plan; the per-tool usage limits that do differ appear only in the table
scorecard.why: Cards don't show why to move up; the differences are buried in the table.

scorecard.key_number: middle plan carries a popularity badge; comparison table present; mobile layout not checked
scorecard.why: The eye is guided to the plan the page wants sold.

scorecard.key_number: a pricing-transparency line under the headline; the only social proof is one general customer claim in the closing banner
scorecard.why: No proof near the plans that teams like the buyer use it.
Nothing manufactured, which is right for this buyer.
Billing, plan changes, limits, plan fit, extra costs and support questions go unanswered on the page.

scorecard.key_number: all 3 plan buttons share one generic start label, also used in the table, the navigation and the closing banner, and all go to the same sign-up page on an app subdomain; no risk-reducing line by the buttons; button contrast unknown (no screenshot)
scorecard.why: Labels don't say which plan the visitor is starting on.

channels.comment: search brings the most pricing visits and they engage well
direct visits engage a little less than search

engagement.note: Scroll fires once at 90% depth, so read-to-bottom means reached the bottom, not a depth curve.

landing_on_pricing.note: under 1.5 pages per session: most visitors who land on pricing see nothing else

new_vs_returning.note: returning visitors spend about 2.6x longer per view than new ones: they come back to compare before buying (reported, not graded)

critical_issues.evidence: Events on the pricing page are only automatic ones plus a custom event that fires about once per session (29 vs 30 session starts). The click report for the page returns 0 rows although outbound clicks are on. Every sign-up link goes to an app subdomain, and GA4 never sends outbound clicks for subdomains. 12 key events are defined; 0 fired in 30 days.
critical_issues.why_it_costs: Without a plan-click event, no test on this page can be read and the funnel stops at a page view.
critical_issues.fix: Send a custom event on every plan button with the plan name as a parameter (site code or tag manager), confirm it fires, then mark it as a key event. Tag the sign-up step with the same property so the sign-up key event can fire.
critical_issues.label: directional: under 100 pricing views

critical_issues.evidence: The page goes from the comparison table to the closing banner with no questions answered. Competitor A answers its buyers' questions in an FAQ under its plans.
critical_issues.why_it_costs: Buyers with a billing, limits or cancellation question have to leave pricing to find the answer, or ask sales.
critical_issues.fix: Add the questions listed under rewrites, right under the plan cards.

improvements.evidence: 12 of 19 next-page views (63%) go to the integrations list; the pricing page shows a capacity number and a "View all" link, not the integrations themselves.
improvements.why_it_costs: Each visitor who leaves to check compatibility is one more step away from choosing a plan.
improvements.fix: Show the most-used integrations as a logo row above or beside the plans, with the full list one click away.
improvements.label: directional: under 100 pricing views

improvements.evidence: Each card lists the same short list; only the capacity, seat and add-on numbers change. The per-tool usage limits that do differ are only in the table.
improvements.why_it_costs: When every card looks alike, the cheapest plan looks like the sensible choice.
improvements.fix: On each card, lead with what the plan adds over the one below (more capacity, more seats, higher usage limits, onboarding), and drop the shared items into one line: "Every plan includes ...".

improvements.evidence: A pricing-transparency line sits under the headline. The only social proof is one general customer claim in the closing banner, below the table.
improvements.why_it_costs: At the moment of choosing a plan, the buyer sees nothing that says teams like theirs rely on it.
improvements.fix: Put real proof beside the plans: customer logos, one short quote from a team like the Plan 2 buyer, or a rating, only what the business can show. Add a plain billing line ("cancel any time") if it's true.

improvements.evidence: The same start label appears on all 3 plan cards, in the comparison-table headers, in the navigation and in the closing banner.
improvements.why_it_costs: A label that is the same everywhere doesn't confirm which plan the click starts.
improvements.fix: Name the plan on each button so the next step is clear (rewrites below).

improvements.evidence: Read-to-bottom is 16% on pricing vs 22% across the site (0.71 of the site rate).
improvements.why_it_costs: The comparison table and the sales path sit where most visitors never arrive.
improvements.fix: Move the sales path and the key table rows (usage limits) higher, and put the new FAQ right under the cards.
improvements.label: directional: under 100 pricing views

improvements.evidence: Daily sessions ran at 0 to 8 until 2026-09-30, then 69 to 99: tracking was only complete for the last 4 days. 4 of the 12 key events are test events.
improvements.why_it_costs: Decisions taken on 4 days of full data can swing on a handful of visits.
improvements.fix: Treat this report as directional, archive the test key events, and rerun after 30 complete days.

tier_by_tier.recommendation: Say who outgrows it and when (the capacity limit), so the step to Plan 2 feels natural.

tier_by_tier.adds_over_plan_below: about 4x capacity, more seats, higher per-tool usage limits (table only)
tier_by_tier.recommendation: Keep the badge; lead the card with what it adds over Plan 1 and show the lower cost per unit.

tier_by_tier.adds_over_plan_below: about 4x capacity, more seats, higher per-tool usage limits (table only)
tier_by_tier.recommendation: Add a sales path on the card itself for buyers who need more than the top plan.

pricing_psychology.note: The top plan sits beside the others at about 10x the entry price.
The middle plan is badged and placed in the middle.
Three plans with a clear middle already steer buyers; don't add a plan just to steer.
The top plan, pitched at established agencies, makes the badged middle plan look like the solid professional choice rather than the cheap one. Keep it visible.
Cost per unit of capacity falls at each step (by about a third, then about a fifth), but the page never says so. Show it on the cards.
Plan prices and add-ons are shown per month, which feels smaller than a yearly total, but the annual saving is shown in months rather than money.
The saving (over 25% off) is shown in months. Test adding the yearly amount saved per plan next to the toggle.
Every price ends just below a round number. For a business buyer, round numbers can read as more confident; worth a test once plan clicks are measured.
None on the page, which is right unless a real past price exists. Never show an invented one.
The page gives no value figure and no comparison with the cost of doing the work another way. Test one value line on the middle plan, using only numbers the business can back.

rewrites.tier_names: Keep. The names say which stage or audience each plan is for.

ab_tests.test: Measurement first: plan-click event plus key event
ab_tests.hypothesis: If every plan button sends an event with the plan name, then plan choices per pricing view become measurable, because today the page records none.
If billing, limits and cancellation questions are answered on the page, then more pricing viewers click a plan, because they no longer leave to find answers.
ab_tests.metric: plan-click events per pricing view; share of next-page views to docs

ab_tests.test: Integration logo row beside the plans
ab_tests.hypothesis: If the main integrations show on the page, then fewer visitors leave for the integrations list (63% of next-page views now, directional) and more click a plan, because the compatibility question is answered in place.
ab_tests.metric: share of next-page views to the integrations list; plan-click rate

ab_tests.test: Cards that lead with what each plan adds
ab_tests.hypothesis: If each card shows its step up (capacity, usage limits, seats, cost per unit) instead of the shared list, then more buyers pick Plan 2 or 3, because the reason to move up is visible.
If each button names its plan, then plan-click rate rises, because the next step is clearer.
